overview: The exact atlas id “nepal” covers 1200 to 1279. Its decoded ten-position polygon is a coarse western Himalayan shape, not modern Nepal. It includes tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini, while excluding Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, and Simraungadh. Period sources usually call the Kathmandu Valley Nepal or Nepal Mandala, while a distinct Khasa kingdom grew around Sinja in the west. Early Valley Malla rulers survive mainly in dated Sanskrit manuscript colophons and later chronicles; western archaeology preserves settlements, pipes, monuments, and routes. These records illuminate courts, donors, monasteries, and ritual places more clearly than most households. Agriculture, craft production, manuscript copying, pilgrimage, and exchange across India and the Tibetan plateau connected communities without making them uniform. Workers, women, and children remain less visible than kings and donors, so daily-life claims are locally bounded and candid about gaps. At 1279 the feature vanishes: tested points become Tibet or Delhi Sultanate colors. This is an atlas seam, not proof of conquest, migration, or social collapse. Separate Nepal ids reappear in 1492 and 1650 as independent snapshots, not automatic successors.

periods.title: 1200 to 1201: an atlas layer meets two histories
periods.summary: The atlas begins a western Himalayan “nepal” polygon, although period Nepal usually meant the Kathmandu Valley. Critical histories place Arimalla at the opening of the Valley's early Malla sequence, while western research identifies a separate Khasa formation around Sinja. The shared word Malla does not make one dynasty.

periods.title: 1201 to 1206: Arimalla enters dated manuscripts
periods.summary: A Sanskrit Sivadharma manuscript copied in 1201 names Arimalladeva's victorious reign and a local official. Its donor Somadeva sought religious benefits for parents, teachers, daughters, sons, and descendants. This is firmer evidence than a later king list, but it describes one commissioned book, not every household.

periods.title: 1206 to 1211: manuscript dates anchor a thin chronology
periods.summary: Petech's reconstruction relies heavily on dated manuscript colophons because narrative sources are scarce. Documents under Arimalla preserve royal titles and copying dates, yet they reveal little about taxation, borders, village government, or succession. The period is historically visible in narrow written beams rather than a fully lit court chronicle.

periods.title: 1211 to 1216: scribes record a reign
periods.summary: A Sanskrit commentary completed in 1216 says it was made during Arimalladeva's reign. Another early thirteenth-century manuscript was produced at Sri Lham Mahavihara for the monk Puspasena, with painted covers. Together they attest learned workshops, patrons, and monasteries without proving broad literacy or one official script.

periods.title: 1216 to 1230: Abhayamalla and uncertain succession
periods.summary: Tribhuvan University and critical chronologies place Abhayamalla after Arimalla, but dates and genealogies vary across manuscripts and later chronicles. The safe lesson is a new royal phase in the Kathmandu Valley amid powerful subordinates. The western Khasa country inside much of the polygon followed a separate political story.

periods.title: 1230 to 1245: sparse royal records
periods.summary: The early Malla record is much thinner than records after the late fourteenth century. Competing chronologies preserve only narrow views of courts and succession. Silence about ordinary people reflects which records survived, not an empty countryside, a uniform society, or a period when everyday work somehow stopped.

periods.title: 1245 to 1255: distinct mountain worlds
periods.summary: Western archaeology places Khasa power along routes linking India and Tibet and distinguishes those rulers from the Valley Mallas. The atlas polygon can introduce this western formation alongside Valley history only when it keeps their courts, communities, and geographies separate rather than merging them through one shared title.

periods.title: 1255 to 1258: earthquake, displacement, and royal death
periods.summary: A Valley chronicle dates an earthquake to 7 June 1255. It says houses and temples fell, survivors lived outdoors, aftershocks continued four months, and Abhayamalla died eight days later. Its one-third mortality fraction is memorable but cannot be treated as a contemporary census.

periods.title: 1258 to 1271: a disputed succession
periods.summary: The years after Abhayamalla have a disputed royal succession reconstructed from colophons and chronicles. Names and dates vary, while ordinary work and local government remain mostly invisible. The safe lesson is continued political uncertainty, not a neat kingdom-wide program or a single sequence accepted by every historian.

periods.title: 1271 to 1279: approaching the seam
periods.summary: By the 1260s and 1270s, the artisan Aniko's career linked a Valley background with Tibet and the Yuan court; a Chinese epitaph is the main source. At Sinja, one excavated phase has a radiocarbon range beginning around 1270 but extending to 1420, so it cannot date every find to this decade.

sections.title: Read the map before trusting the label

items.text: The live index contains one exact id, “nepal,” named “Nepal,” with approximate coverage from 1200 to 1279. One border file carries it, while the exact card, review, and researched override remain missing. The imported summary describes today's multilingual country and is not valid copy for a medieval feature.

The 1200 feature is one Polygon, one ring, and ten decoded positions. Its bbox is 80.10260102601029, 27.27706261766734 to 85.86265862658627, 30.191319255656083; its decoded geometry SHA-256 is f4d85a7e28dba748287fe20d271edaa82f049f6a2a7ca68ed3b9308dc25d0a66. These are reproducible display-data facts, not surveyed medieval borders or sovereignty coordinates.

Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini fall inside. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, and the Khasa-Tatopani crossing do not. The shape therefore emphasizes western hills while excluding the Kathmandu Valley historical core discussed by most early Malla sources.

At 1200 the target directly shares encoded arcs with the atlas's “tibet” and “delhi-sultanate” features. Kathmandu and its neighboring Valley cities lie in the Tibet color, while southern lowland probes lie in the Delhi Sultanate color. Shared arcs and fills describe this dataset, not actual tribute, occupation, language, or religion.

The later ids “nepal-1492” and “nepal-1650” are separate indexed records, not automatic successors. The 1492 shape repeats the coarse western footprint; the 1650 shape changes its northern edge. Both again omit the tested Valley core. Reused coloring cannot turn three intermittent snapshots into one continuously bounded state.

sections.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach

items.text: Arimalla is the first ruler in this sequence regularly associated with the Malla title, but “Malla” meant a prestigious title rather than proof that every later namesake belonged to one family. Kathmandu Valley Mallas and western Khasa Mallas must remain separate. Their overlapping labels are a historian's trap with excellent branding.

The 1201 Sivadharma colophon gives Arimalladeva elaborate Shaiva royal titles and names Ranaka Haridharasimha as an official. Such formulae show how authority was announced through religion and local office. They do not reveal the actual reach of commands, tax collection, or control across the atlas's western polygon.

Critical chronology for 1200 to 1279 is assembled from manuscript dates, inscriptions, and chronicles copied later. Sources become substantially richer only after this card's interval. Exact regnal lists vary, so the card uses broad teaching phases and identifies uncertainty instead of pretending that a tidy modern timeline survived from every court.

Western Khasa rulers established seasonal centers around Sinja and Dullu during the thirteenth century. Archaeology and inscriptions frame a regional formation tied to pilgrimage and mountain routes. That history fits much of the drawn polygon better than Valley Malla history, yet it still cannot certify the atlas line as a Khasa frontier.

Sinja and Kathmandu were not interchangeable capitals. Nepal's Department of Archaeology describes Sinja as a western Khasa center, while the atlas audit places Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur outside this polygon. Political power, landscape, and surviving evidence differ; “Nepal” is an editorial doorway, not one palace speaking for everyone.

sections.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work

items.text: A broad history links medieval Valley agriculture, craft work, and trade, but most of its economic evidence comes from later Malla centuries. It supplies questions about cultivators and artisans, not a measured 1200 harvest, crop list, household budget, or proof that the western hills followed the same pattern.

Bhaktapur's long-lived water system linked canals, stone spouts, ponds, household supply, and cultivation. The study traces change and reuse across centuries, so continuity into 1200 to 1279 is context rather than a complete period map. It cannot name every working channel or each family responsible for maintenance.

Sankhu lay on an old route from the Kathmandu Valley toward Tibet. Pack animals, porters, religious travelers, artisans, and merchants made such links work, although route studies rarely preserve their names or wages. A connected road did not erase different languages, authorities, or local risks along the journey.

Aniko's later epitaph places the Valley-trained artisan in Tibet and at the Yuan court. Elite commissions moved skills across mountains, but his exceptional career cannot establish ordinary mobility or wages. One famous traveler did not make every craft worker an international commuter.

The 1316 epitaph places Aniko in Tibet and at the Yuan court during this interval. His exceptional mobility shows elite commissions moving skills across mountains. It cannot represent an ordinary craft career, and modern national borders should not be inserted into his thirteenth-century journey.

sections.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work

items.text: The 1255 chronicle says many houses and temples collapsed and survivors lived outside for weeks. It does not describe floor plans, roofing, ownership, or whether households shared courtyards. The disaster makes ordinary shelter briefly visible, but its silence prevents one “typical Nepali house” from being invented across western hills and the Valley.

An architectural study shows how famous Valley buildings combine old traditions, rebuilding, and uncertain dates. Its careful separation of surviving fabric from legends is more useful than declaring every brick wall or carved timber medieval. It offers construction context, not a typical thirteenth-century floor plan or household inventory.

At Sinja, excavators found building cells, thresholds, paths, pits, pottery, glass, and animal bone. One relevant radiocarbon range begins around 1270 but runs to 1420, and later occupation complicates the assemblage. These finds illuminate tasks and rooms near the seam without furnishing a household inventory for the whole 1200 to 1279 period.

A broad history attributes cotton spinning, weaving, metalwork, woodwork, and trade to medieval Valley households and specialists. Most supporting detail comes from later Malla centuries. For this card, it shows enduring occupational traditions worth investigating, while clothing cuts, loom ownership, work hours, and gendered labor in 1200 remain insufficiently documented.

Sinja excavations recovered pottery and animal bone, but mixed phases prevent a dependable 1200 to 1279 menu. The finds show food-related activity only broadly; they do not place modern dal bhat on every thirteenth-century plate. History should ask before raiding someone's lunchbox.

sections.title: Families, status, belief, and social life

items.text: Somadeva's 1201 manuscript donation names benefits sought for mother, father, teachers, daughters, sons, and grandchildren. That makes kin and teaching relationships directly visible in a dated source. Because this is a learned donor's religious commission, it cannot define marriage, inheritance, household size, or affection for every social group.

The painted manuscript from Sri Lham Mahavihara names the monk Puspasena as its recipient and locates skilled work inside a religious institution. It reveals patronage and institutional relationships, not the monk's household, childhood, or daily timetable. Even a splendid book leaves most social life outside its covers.

Shaiva and Buddhist manuscript production overlapped rather than forming sealed populations. Arimalla's royal titles invoke Shiva and Pashupati, while Sri Lham Mahavihara produced a painted Buddhist book for monk Puspasena. Elite religious sources reveal plural patronage, but they leave household practice, local deities, and disagreement only partly visible.

Sankhu's nomination describes an old settlement on the Valley-to-Tibet route, but its prominent surviving Vajrayogini complex is largely seventeenth century. A sacred place could gather residents, pilgrims, workers, and traders without preserving their conversations. Long continuity must not turn later buildings into a 1200 street scene.

Early Malla histories favor rulers, titles, officials, and manuscript dates. Farmers, herders, porters, servants, women outside donor formulas, and lower-status workers rarely appear by name. Imbalance matters: silence in court-centered chronology is not absence from society or a population census.

sections.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample

items.text: No reviewed source preserves a typical child's timetable, games, chores, or age at apprenticeship between 1200 and 1279. Manuscripts demonstrate teachers, monks, scribes, and learned patrons; craft careers imply training. They do not establish universal schooling, literacy rates, or equal access for girls, rural children, and lower-status families.

A 1316 Chinese epitaph tells how the young Aniko studied texts, calligraphy, painting, modeling, and casting before traveling. The account concerns an exceptional artisan and was written after his death. It is delightful evidence for an idealized child prodigy, not proof that every seven-year-old had bronze repair homework.

The dated Valley manuscripts used here are Sanskrit, while Sinja's institutional nomination records thirteenth-century Devanagari-script evidence in the western center. Script, language, place, and genre must remain separate: a court colophon or inscription cannot establish what every porter, farmer, child, or craft worker spoke at home.

Written-language sample, Nepalese manuscript, 1 January 1216: “राज्ये ह्यरिमल्लदेवीये” (rājye hy arimalladevīye), “during the reign of Arimalladeva.” The source prints a normalized Devanagari transcription of a Sanskrit colophon, not a facsimile of the original hand. Its exact copying workshop or Valley locality is not identified.

A University of Pennsylvania leaf preserves Sanskrit from the Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita and is broadly dated 1200 to 1399; painted images were added over the writing later. That range is too wide to call the leaf a 1200 to 1279 product. It does show why text, painting, and object date must be separated.

A palm-leaf Susrutasamhita copied in Nepal in 878 preserves a major Sanskrit medical text. The institutional record establishes learned medical writing centuries before this card, but not which thirteenth-century healers read it, which treatments they used, or whether ordinary patients could reach a manuscript-trained practitioner.

The institutional record describes the 878 medical manuscript as covering surgery and diseases involving skin, heart, gynecology, and other fields. Those are topics in a learned text, not clinical outcomes from 1200 to 1279. Preserved knowledge and everyday practice must remain separate unless a securely dated local medical record connects them.

The 1255 earthquake account implies crush injuries, exposure, bereavement, disrupted water, and prolonged fear as aftershocks continued. Yet it names no hospital, physician, medicine, or organized relief. The honest health history therefore describes hazards and source silence rather than importing a fully documented emergency service into the medieval Valley.

The reviewed medical manuscript record supplies no securely dated 1200 to 1279 patient case, physician's kit, prescription, hospital register, or childbirth account. That is a survival problem, not evidence that care did not exist. Family help, ritual care, herbs, and specialists remain possible but unquantified.

Water infrastructure affected health even though its builders did not use germ theory. Channels, recharge ponds, tanks, and stone spouts helped move water toward fields and settlements, but the sources provide no thirteenth-century water-quality tests or equal-access survey. A beautiful spout could still demand cleaning, repair, and fair distribution.

sections.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question

items.text: An architectural study of two Valley buildings separates documented water structures from legends and later rebuilding. That matters because spouts, tanks, shrines, and masonry changed across centuries. Surviving water architecture shows continuity, but not that every component worked unchanged in 1200 or reached every household equally.

Bhaktapur research describes cascaded reuse: water moved among domestic supply, recharge, and cultivation rather than entering one modern sewer. That helps explain labor around collection and maintenance. The study examines a long-lived system, however, and cannot tell us the exact bucket route, cleaning roster, or neighborhood access in 1237.

At Sinja, archaeological survey recorded an earthen pipe system among the capital's remains. Its elements are not all securely dated inside 1200 to 1279. The pipes demonstrate water engineering in the western center, but neither their full route nor a thirteenth-century maintenance organization is securely reconstructed.

No reviewed source securely identifies a 1200 to 1279 latrine, toilet seat, cesspit, chamber pot, or rule for disposing of human waste in these communities. Drains and spouts managed water, but a drain is not automatically a toilet. Medieval plumbing deserves credit without receiving imaginary porcelain accessories.

The reviewed water study describes channels, spouts, ponds, recharge, reuse, and maintenance, but it does not identify a thirteenth-century rubbish route, sewage service, cleaning roster, or neighborhood sanitation rule. Those absences matter: a sophisticated water network did not automatically provide every modern municipal service.

sections.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement

items.text: A thirteenth-century Kathmandu Valley ritual-vessel handle is cast in copper alloy as five intertwined nagas with human torsos, snake hoods, jewels, crowns, and extended bodies. The object demonstrates sophisticated openwork metal craft and water symbolism. Its museum record does not identify the workshop, patron, wage, or user's household.

A thirteenth-century Valley image of Lakshmi combines copper alloy with semiprecious-stone inlay. It is strong evidence for casting, finishing, stone setting, and religious patronage, but weak evidence for production volume or artisan status. A surviving masterpiece is the opposite of an average object; museums are excellent at keeping overachievers.

Sri Lham Mahavihara produced an early thirteenth-century Sanskrit manuscript for the monk Puspasena with striking painted wooden covers. The colophon names the monastery as a great monastery of an auspicious great image. That joins calligraphy, painting, woodworking, religious donation, and institutional life in one securely period-bound object.

The 1216 Harihara commentary survives with a dated post-colophon tied to Arimalladeva's reign. Producing a manuscript required prepared writing material, ink, a trained hand, exemplars, checking, and patronage. Copying was skilled labor as well as learning; a ruler's date formula should not make the scribe's material work disappear.

Sankhu preserves a long settlement and pilgrimage history, but its nomination dates the prominent Vajrayogini temple complex chiefly to the seventeenth century. This card therefore gives priority to dated thirteenth-century manuscripts and objects. Famous later buildings illustrate continuity and rebuilding, not an unchanged photograph of 1200.

sections.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam

items.text: Sinja's ridge includes large ditches, ramparts, a monumental gateway approach, and defensive interpretations, but excavators repeatedly stress ambiguous dates and later building. Fortifications redirect paths, demand labor, and shelter some people while burdening others. They do not by themselves prove a particular battle inside 1200 to 1279.

Khasa expansion linked western hill centers, pilgrimage places, and routes, yet political growth could affect cultivators, carriers, ritual communities, and chiefs differently. Inscriptions usually praise rulers and donations rather than list displaced families. Warfare and negotiation must therefore be described as community pressures without inventing a casualty total or ethnic bloc.

The 1255 earthquake was not warfare, but it was the interval's clearest mass danger. Houses and temples fell, the king died, and survivors stayed outside while aftershocks continued. Women, children, servants, laborers, monks, and marginalized residents are not separately counted; the chronicle's collective suffering hides unequal exposure.

At the exact 1279 seam, “nepal” disappears. Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla switch to the atlas's Tibet color, while Doti and Lumbini switch to Delhi Sultanate; the same ownership persists in 1300. These are software layers with no encoded conquest event, migration, royal death, or social rupture.

Later “nepal-1492” and “nepal-1650” records reappear after gaps of 213 and 150 years. They are not named as successors in this card because intermittent reuse of a label does not establish one continuous state. Farms, routes, workshops, water systems, families, languages, and religious communities continued through the 1279 display seam.

ending.text: At 1279 the exact “nepal” feature disappears: tested member points are reassigned to the atlas's Tibet and Delhi Sultanate layers, with no encoded conquest or population break. The 1300 snapshot keeps those colors. Separate Nepal ids return for 1492 to 1500 and 1650 to 1700, after long gaps, and cannot be treated as automatic successors. The override therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor. Valley and western courts changed, while households, farming, routes, crafts, manuscripts, religious institutions, water systems, and languages continued through the editorial seam.
